# INVALID ESCAPES. Both runtimes reject these; neither used to.
# `\xAg` was `{"a":"\n"}` in TypeScript: parseInt is not a validator -- it
# stops at the first non-hex character and returns what it read, so `Ag`
# decoded as 0x0A and the `g` vanished. Go's strconv.ParseInt errors, which is
# why only one runtime was wrong. `\xA"` is the same defect eating the CLOSING
# QUOTE, which is why it used to surface as unterminated_string instead of a
# bad escape.
# `\UFFFFFFFF` was a REPLACEMENT CHARACTER in a successful Go parse --
# WriteRune above 0x10FFFF does not fail, it silently writes U+FFFD -- and in
# TypeScript it was an uncaught RangeError from String.fromCodePoint, reported
# as `unexpected`: a crash wearing a diagnostic's clothes, and the reason the
# isUnicodeCharacter check below it never ran.
a = "\xAg"
